summary:
SPHEREx photographs the entire sky every six months. Its public archive already holds 1.6 million images, and anything that moves across them, such as asteroids, comets, nearby brown dwarfs or perhaps an unknown planet, hides among millions of fixed stars. Finding it means comparing the same patch of sky across months. Today, that requires downloading files and writing code.

SkySwap turns this archive into a public web app that anyone can scroll. Each profile is a real object in the sky. Photos taken months apart blink on screen, and people answer one question: did something move? Answers are blind, so no one sees what others said. When five careful answers agree, the patch becomes a candidate, and the app checks it against known catalogs. Any coordinate can be opened, played as a time-lapse and compared with WISE images from 15 years earlier. The spectrum is translated into plain words, such as water, methane or carbon dioxide.

SkySwap does not claim discoveries. It shows where to look, labels every machine guess as a guess, and leaves the final check to people. Real data. Real people. Find what moves.
details:
The problem

Anything that moves across the sky gives itself away the same way: it changes position between two photos. SPHEREx photographs the whole sky every six months, so its archive is the right place to look for asteroids, comets, nearby brown dwarfs or a distant planet. The archive, however, is built for specialists. A single image is a 2040 × 2040 pixel file with several layers, and comparing one patch of sky across months means finding the right files, cutting the same region from each one and lining them up. SkySwap removes every one of those steps.

What SkySwap does

SkySwap is a public web app with the shape of a social feed. Each profile is a real object in the sky, and the photos are real SPHEREx images. Five features carry the project.

1. Swap.
Photos of the same patch taken months apart blink on screen. People answer one question: did something move? A tap marks where, with a magnifier for precision. Answers are blind. Nobody sees what others said, and a patch that becomes a finding leaves the deck of anyone who saw the discussion first.

2. Findings.
When five careful answers agree, the patch becomes a candidate. The app then checks it against known catalogs: fast-moving stars from Gaia, known objects from SIMBAD and asteroids predicted for that date. The result is shown as "already known" or "open". A community tab lists the open candidates and hosts the discussion.

3. Any point in the sky.
Any coordinate can be opened, played as a time-lapse and compared with older WISE and 2MASS images of the same place. A link reopens exactly the same view, so a finding can be shared.

4. Spectrum in plain words.
SPHEREx sees each point in many infrared colors. The app measures them and writes the result in words. For Epsilon Indi B it shows water, methane and carbon monoxide. For the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, the carbon dioxide band shines about 40 times brighter than the light next to it.

5. Lab.
A workbench for people who want to measure. It stacks photos to reveal faint sources, stacks them along a motion to reveal faint moving objects, measures brightness over time and shows the quality flags of every pixel.

How it works

The system has four parts, shown in Figure 1.


1. A sky index built for the browser.
Our pipeline read the headers of every public SPHEREx image: 1,628,230 images from the DR1 and QR3 releases. It split the sky into 12,288 equal cells (HEALPix) and wrote one small file per cell. The first version repeated each image in every cell it touched and reached 12.2 GB. A two-part format stores each image once, with a light file per cell and the heavy details per image, and fell to 1.6 GB. A validator compared both formats row by row: 16.1 million rows, zero differences. Opening a point now downloads about 336 KB.

2. Photos read from NASA's own archive.
The app never copies the images. It reads only the bytes it needs from the public archive, crops the exact region on screen and sends it compressed. A photo that used to cost 3.9 MB now costs 21 KB, with identical pixels. On a slow mobile network, the first photo arrives in about 4 seconds.

3. Science measured in advance for the featured objects.
For each object, the pipeline gathers every photo, follows moving bodies with JPL Horizons ephemerides, measures brightness, position and spectrum, and builds the Lab packages.

4. The app.
A phone-first web app that also works with keyboard and mouse, in English and Portuguese. It has stories, profiles, the swap deck, the community and the Lab. Image processing for the Lab runs inside the browser.

How we kept the science honest

Every number shown in the app was tested against cases with a known answer. Four checks matter most.

- Spectral features: count only when the signal passes five times its uncertainty and agrees across most of the band. On the 36 objects, they found the expected molecules in brown dwarfs and the CO and CO₂ emission in comets, and stayed silent on asteroids and plain stars.

- Bright stars: saturate the camera. For five of them, the app measures the scattered light around the center instead. On Algol, the photos taken during predicted eclipses dropped to half the brightness. On Delta Cephei, the 5.4-day pulse appeared with the expected size.

- The machine guesses: that help people look are labeled as guesses. They count a motion only above five times the jitter of nearby still stars. In a test on 20 random patches of sky, the robot flagged 2: one was the known asteroid (2913) Horta, and the other matched nothing known.

- No discovery claims. A candidate stays a candidate until a person checks it.


Tools we built

Seven tools came out of the project:

- the sky index builder;

- its two-part storage format;

- a row-by-row validator;

- the object pipeline (coverage, measurements, spectral features, halo brightness);

- the Lab package builder;

- an in-browser image library for SPHEREx files (cropping, quality masks, wavelength per pixel, stacking);

- a weekly updater that finds new NASA images, refreshes only what changed and publishes it. With nothing new, it runs in about five minutes.

Stack

- Python with Astropy, NumPy and Apache Arrow/Parquet for the pipeline;

- TypeScript with Next.js and React for the app, with WebGPU for in-browser processing;

- Node.js with Fastify and SQLite for the API;

- public data from NASA/IPAC IRSA, Gaia, SIMBAD, JPL Horizons and WISE.

The app runs at zero hosting cost: the interface on Vercel, the API on a free Google Cloud instance and the sky index on Cloudflare R2. (So, unfortunately, it might just collapse under even a slight overload :c)

Factors we considered

- Accessibility. Plain language everywhere, no jargon without explanation, phone first.

- Privacy. Sign-in uses passkeys and a QR code, with no email, phone or name stored. (Perhaps an excuse to reduce the cost)

- Fair participation. No leaderboards of people, and no feature locked behind a level.

- Scientific images are never cropped for looks.

- Sustainability. Small files, compressed crops and a free stack, so the project can stay online.


Impact

SkySwap lets anyone take part in the search for moving objects with real, current data. It also turns the SPHEREx archive into something a curious person can explore in seconds. It does not replace professional pipelines. It adds many careful human eyes to the parts of the sky that need them.

Real data. Real people. Find what moves.
